summary.one_liner: mal (Make a Lisp) is a Clojure-inspired Lisp interpreter built as a learning tool, implemented in dozens of host languages across 11 incremental steps.
summary.what_it_does: The repository contains mal, a Clojure-inspired Lisp, implemented separately in 89 languages (95 implementations, 118 runtime modes) under impls/. Each implementation is split into 11 incremental, testable steps (step0_repl through stepA_mal) that introduce core Lisp concepts such as read/print, eval, environments, if/fn/do, tail-call optimization, file loading, quoting, macros, and try/catch. The final step is self-hosting, meaning mal can run its own mal implementation. A shared test suite of almost 800 functional tests in tests/ can be run against any implementation, and the top-level Makefile provides targets for REPLs, performance tests, language statistics, and Docker-based runs. Several related projects are listed, including a Mal-to-LLVM compiler, a Tiny C Compiler backend, and a Mal-to-Python compiler.
use_cases: learn how interpreters and Lisp evaluators work
step-by-step tutorial for writing a Lisp in another language
compare language implementations side by side
run a small Clojure-style Lisp REPL
test an interpreter against a shared functional test suite
how_to_run: make "test^IMPL" to test one implementation, or make test for all
stack: Many host languages including Ada, C, C++, Go, Haskell, Java, JavaScript/Node, Python, Ruby, Rust, Swift, WebAssembly (Wam)
notable: Same Lisp implemented in 89 languages, each with the same 11 incremental steps
Self-hosting: the final step can run mal's own mal implementation
Shared test suite of almost 800 functional tests across all implementations
Docker images per implementation for building and testing without local toolchains
Includes a Clojure-flavoured PHP project (frock) and a Mal-to-LLVM compiler among related projects
caveats: Runtime performance is explicitly not a primary goal; the performance tests are described as neither statistically valid nor comprehensive
Some implementations need specific or proprietary tooling: MATLAB is commercial, the Q implementation needs a manual download and is kept separately, and Swift 2 is no longer easily buildable
Several implementations are tied to old toolchain versions (e.g. Julia 0.4, Clojure 1.5, Python2) and may not build on current systems
